_about: Short editorial notes written for the Open Wine Atlas. Each note is matched to a place by id, or by country + name. Facts here are general wine knowledge and should be checked against the official specification before reuse. Licence: CC BY 4.0, Open Wine Atlas contributors.

notes.name: Chambertin
notes.note: Grand cru of Gevrey-Chambertin and one of the most powerful, long-lived red Burgundies. Pinot Noir on a gentle mid-slope of limestone and marl, just below the woods. Long associated with Napoleon, who is said to have drunk little else. The mapped area also includes Chambertin-Clos de Bèze, whose wine may be sold as Chambertin.

notes.name: Chambertin-Clos de Bèze
notes.note: Grand cru adjoining Chambertin to the north. The monks of the Abbey of Bèze planted a vineyard here in the 7th century, which makes it one of the oldest named sites in Burgundy. It may legally be sold as Chambertin, but not the other way round.

notes.name: Mazis-Chambertin
notes.note: Grand cru on the north side of Gevrey, just above the village road. Usually firm and dark-fruited, with a reputation for depth close to Chambertin itself.

notes.name: Ruchottes-Chambertin
notes.note: One of the smallest grands crus of Gevrey, high on the slope above Mazis. Thin, stony soils over limestone give a taut, mineral style.

notes.name: Latricières-Chambertin
notes.note: Grand cru south of Chambertin on the border with Morey-Saint-Denis. A cool air corridor from the Combe Grisard is often cited for its fresher, more linear style.

notes.name: Charmes-Chambertin
notes.note: The largest grand cru of Gevrey, below Chambertin across the Route des Grands Crus. Wine from Mazoyères-Chambertin may be sold under this name, which is why Charmes is far more common on labels. The mapped area therefore includes Mazoyères.

notes.name: Mazoyères-Chambertin
notes.note: Grand cru below Latricières. Its wines may be labelled Charmes-Chambertin, so the Mazoyères name is rarely seen.

notes.name: Chapelle-Chambertin
notes.note: Grand cru south of Clos de Bèze, below the road. Shallow soils give a perfumed, more delicate Chambertin style.

notes.name: Griotte-Chambertin
notes.note: The smallest grand cru of Gevrey, set in a slight hollow next to Chapelle. Prized for an intensely fruity, cherry-scented profile that matches its name.

notes.name: Clos de la Roche
notes.note: The largest grand cru of Morey-Saint-Denis, on limestone close to the surface. Often described as the most structured of the Morey grands crus.

notes.name: Clos Saint-Denis
notes.note: Grand cru that gave its name to the village of Morey-Saint-Denis. Known for finesse and aromatic lift rather than sheer weight.

notes.name: Clos des Lambrays
notes.note: Grand cru of Morey-Saint-Denis, promoted in 1981 and almost entirely owned by one domaine, Domaine des Lambrays, which belongs to LVMH since 2014.

notes.name: Clos de Tart
notes.note: Walled grand cru monopole of Morey-Saint-Denis, never divided since the 12th century. Bought in 2017 by Artémis, the Pinault family's holding. Rows run across the slope, unusual for the Côte.

notes.name: Bonnes-Mares
notes.note: Grand cru shared between Morey-Saint-Denis and Chambolle-Musigny. Growers distinguish darker 'terres rouges' and paler, chalkier 'terres blanches', which shape a wine that is both firm and fragrant.

notes.name: Musigny
notes.note: Grand cru of Chambolle-Musigny and a benchmark for silky, perfumed Pinot Noir. One of very few grands crus of the Côte de Nuits that also produces white wine, in tiny quantities from Chardonnay.

notes.name: Clos de Vougeot
notes.note: About 50 ha enclosed by a wall built by the Cistercian monks of Cîteaux from the 12th century. Today shared by around 80 owners, so quality depends on the producer and on where the parcel lies, from the upper slope down to the road. The château is the seat of the Confrérie des Chevaliers du Tastevin.

notes.name: Échezeaux
notes.note: Large grand cru in the commune of Flagey-Échezeaux, sold with the wines of Vosne-Romanée. The many lieux-dits inside it vary a lot, which makes producer choice important.

notes.name: Grands-Échezeaux
notes.note: Grand cru next to Clos de Vougeot, lower and more homogeneous than Échezeaux. Usually deeper and more complete than its larger neighbour.

notes.name: Romanée-Conti
notes.note: Grand cru monopole of about 1.8 ha owned by the Domaine de la Romanée-Conti. Named after the Prince de Conti, who bought it in 1760. Its wine is among the most sought-after in the world.

notes.name: La Tâche
notes.note: Grand cru monopole of the Domaine de la Romanée-Conti in Vosne-Romanée. Richer and more spicy than Romanée-Conti, and one of the reference points of the Côte de Nuits.

notes.name: Richebourg
notes.note: Grand cru of Vosne-Romanée north of Romanée-Conti. Known for opulence and depth, with several famous owners sharing it.

notes.name: Romanée-Saint-Vivant
notes.note: Grand cru below Romanée-Conti, named after the monks of the priory of Saint-Vivant. Deeper soils give a more floral, ethereal style than its neighbours.

notes.name: La Romanée
notes.note: Often cited as the smallest appellation in France, under one hectare. A monopole of the Comte Liger-Belair, just above Romanée-Conti.

notes.name: La Grande Rue
notes.note: Narrow strip between La Tâche and Romanée-Conti, a monopole of Domaine François Lamarche. It became a grand cru in 1992.

notes.name: Corton
notes.note: The largest grand cru of Burgundy and the only red grand cru of the Côte de Beaune, on the hill of Corton shared by Aloxe-Corton, Ladoix-Serrigny and Pernand-Vergelesses. A climat name can be added, such as Corton Bressandes or Corton Clos du Roi.

notes.name: Corton-Charlemagne
notes.note: White grand cru on the upper slopes of the hill of Corton, planted with Chardonnay. Tradition links it to the emperor Charlemagne, who is said to have owned vines here.

notes.name: Montrachet
notes.note: Grand cru shared by Puligny-Montrachet and Chassagne-Montrachet and widely seen as the greatest site for Chardonnay. Around 8 ha, at the heart of a family of five grands crus that carry the Montrachet name.

notes.name: Chevalier-Montrachet
notes.note: Grand cru directly above Montrachet in Puligny. Steeper and stonier, it gives a tighter, more mineral wine.

notes.name: Bâtard-Montrachet
notes.note: Grand cru below Montrachet, across the path, shared by Puligny and Chassagne. Deeper soils give a broad, rich white Burgundy.

notes.name: Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet
notes.note: Small grand cru in Puligny-Montrachet, carved out of the north-east corner of Bâtard-Montrachet.

notes.name: Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet
notes.note: The smallest of the Montrachet grands crus, in Chassagne-Montrachet, just south of Bâtard.

notes.name: Chablis Grand Cru
notes.note: One appellation made of seven climats on a single south-west facing slope above the town of Chablis, on the right bank of the Serein: Blanchot, Bougros, Les Clos, Grenouilles, Preuses, Valmur and Vaudésir. Chardonnay on Kimmeridgian marl and limestone.

notes.name: Chablis
notes.note: Chardonnay grown around the town of Chablis in the Yonne, the northern outpost of Burgundy. The best sites lie on Kimmeridgian marl with fossil oyster shells, which many link to the wine's saline, chalky edge.

notes.name: Gevrey-Chambertin
notes.note: The largest village of the Côte de Nuits, home to nine grands crus. Its reds are often the most structured of the Côte, with Clos Saint-Jacques as the most famous premier cru.

notes.name: Morey-Saint-Denis
notes.note: Village between Gevrey and Chambolle with five grands crus, among them two monopoles, Clos de Tart and almost all of Clos des Lambrays.

notes.name: Chambolle-Musigny
notes.note: Village famed for the most perfumed and silky reds of the Côte de Nuits. Limestone-rich soils with little clay. Les Amoureuses is its most celebrated premier cru.

notes.name: Vosne-Romanée
notes.note: Village with the highest concentration of grands crus in Burgundy, including Romanée-Conti and La Tâche. Its premiers crus, such as Cros Parantoux, are among the most sought-after in the region.

notes.name: Nuits-Saint-Georges
notes.note: The town that gives the Côte de Nuits its name. No grand cru, but a long list of premiers crus, Les Saint-Georges being the most famous. Reds tend to be firm and earthy.

notes.name: Meursault
notes.note: The largest white-wine village of the Côte de Beaune. No grand cru, but top premiers crus such as Perrières, Charmes and Genevrières give rich, nutty Chardonnay.

notes.name: Puligny-Montrachet
notes.note: Village shared with Chassagne for Montrachet and Bâtard-Montrachet, and home to Chevalier-Montrachet and Bienvenues. Its whites are known for precision and floral tension.

notes.name: Chassagne-Montrachet
notes.note: Southern neighbour of Puligny, with a share of Montrachet and Bâtard and all of Criots-Bâtard. Known for whites, it also produces a good share of red.

notes.name: Volnay
notes.note: Côte de Beaune village known for delicate, perfumed reds. Premiers crus such as Clos des Chênes, Caillerets and Taillepieds are on lighter, limestone-rich soils.

notes.name: Pommard
notes.note: Côte de Beaune village for firm, dark reds. Rugiens and Épenots are its most famous premiers crus, and growers are pushing for grand cru status.

notes.name: Beaune
notes.note: Wine capital of Burgundy and home of the Hospices de Beaune auction. A large number of premiers crus, many owned by the old négociant houses.

notes.name: Champagne
notes.note: Sparkling wine made by second fermentation in bottle, from Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier on chalk and marl. The historic échelle des crus ranks 17 villages as grand cru and 42 as premier cru.

notes.name: Pauillac
notes.note: Médoc commune with three of the five first growths of the 1855 classification: Lafite Rothschild, Latour and Mouton Rothschild. Cabernet Sauvignon on deep gravel gives powerful, long-lived wines.

notes.name: Margaux
notes.note: Médoc appellation covering five communes, with more classified growths from 1855 than any other. Château Margaux is the first growth. The wines are known for fragrance and finesse.

notes.name: Saint-Julien
notes.note: Compact Médoc commune between Pauillac and Margaux, with no first growth but a remarkable run of second growths, such as the three Léovilles and Ducru-Beaucaillou.

notes.name: Saint-Estèphe
notes.note: The northernmost of the great Médoc communes. More clay in the soil than further south gives firmer wines, with Cos d'Estournel and Montrose as leading estates.

notes.name: Pessac-Léognan
notes.note: Appellation created in 1987 from the northern part of the Graves, south of Bordeaux city. Home of Château Haut-Brion, the only first growth outside the Médoc in 1855, and of fine dry whites.

notes.name: Saint-Émilion grand cru
notes.note: Right-bank appellation around the medieval town of Saint-Émilion, dominated by Merlot and Cabernet Franc on limestone plateau, slopes and sand. It has its own classification, revised about every ten years.

notes.name: Pomerol
notes.note: Small right-bank plateau of clay and gravel, mostly planted with Merlot. Pomerol has no official classification, yet it is home to Pétrus and Le Pin.

notes.name: Sauternes
notes.note: Sweet white wine from grapes affected by noble rot, helped by autumn mists from the Ciron river. Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle. Château d'Yquem was the only Premier Cru Supérieur in 1855.

notes.name: Côte Rôtie
notes.note: Steep terraces on the right bank of the Rhône, the northernmost cru of the Rhône valley. Syrah, which may be co-fermented with a small share of Viognier. The Côte Brune and Côte Blonde are its most famous slopes.

notes.name: Condrieu
notes.note: Northern Rhône appellation for white wine from Viognier only, grown on steep granite terraces. Château-Grillet is a separate appellation inside it.

notes.name: Hermitage
notes.note: Granite hill above Tain-l'Hermitage facing south over the Rhône. Syrah for the reds, Marsanne and Roussanne for the whites. One of the oldest famous wine names in France.

notes.name: Cornas
notes.note: Northern Rhône appellation for red wine from Syrah only, on steep granite slopes in a sheltered amphitheatre.

notes.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
notes.note: Southern Rhône appellation where Baron Le Roy drafted rules in the 1920s that inspired the French AOC system. A long list of permitted varieties, Grenache leading, on soils that range from large round stones to sand and limestone.

notes.name: Gigondas
notes.note: Southern Rhône red at the foot of the Dentelles de Montmirail, mostly Grenache with Syrah and Mourvèdre, from higher, cooler vineyards than the valley floor.

notes.name: Sancerre
notes.note: Upper Loire appellation for Sauvignon Blanc, with some Pinot Noir. Three main soil types: terres blanches (Kimmeridgian marl), caillottes (limestone pebbles) and silex (flint).

notes.name: Pouilly-Fumé
notes.note: Sauvignon Blanc from the right bank of the Loire facing Sancerre. Flint-rich soils are often credited for its smoky note.

notes.name: Vouvray
notes.note: Chenin Blanc east of Tours on tuffeau limestone, made from dry to sweet and as sparkling wine. Many producers age wine in caves dug into the tuffeau.

notes.name: Savennières
notes.note: Anjou appellation for dry Chenin Blanc on schist and volcanic rock on the north bank of the Loire. Known for intensity and long ageing.

notes.name: Savennières Coulée de Serrant
notes.note: Monopole inside Savennières owned by the Joly family. Nicolas Joly is one of the pioneers of biodynamic viticulture.

notes.name: Chinon
notes.note: Touraine appellation, mainly red from Cabernet Franc, on gravel near the Vienne river and on limestone slopes inland.

notes.name: Muscadet Sèvre et Maine
notes.note: Melon de Bourgogne near Nantes, at the western end of the Loire. Often aged on its lees, 'sur lie'. Named crus communaux such as Clisson and Gorges are among its sub-zones.

notes.name: Château-Chalon
notes.note: Jura appellation for vin jaune only: Savagnin aged at least six years under a veil of yeast, without topping up, and sold in the 62 cl clavelin bottle.

notes.name: Bandol
notes.note: Provence appellation on terraces above the Mediterranean. Reds and rosés built on Mourvèdre, which needs the warmth and sea exposure of this coast.

notes.name: Alsace
notes.note: Alsace lies in the rain shadow of the Vosges, one of the driest regions of France. Wines are labelled by grape variety, and the 51 grand cru sites each have their own appellation.

notes.name: Barolo
notes.note: Nebbiolo from eleven communes in the Langhe hills south of Alba. At least 38 months of ageing, 18 in wood. Since 2010 single-vineyard names follow an official list of Menzioni Geografiche Aggiuntive (MGA), such as Cannubi or Brunate.

notes.name: Barbaresco
notes.note: Nebbiolo from Barbaresco, Neive, Treiso and part of Alba, north-east of Barolo. At least 26 months of ageing, 9 in wood. Usually a little earlier to approach than Barolo. Single sites follow an official MGA list.

notes.name: Brunello di Montalcino
notes.note: 100% Sangiovese from the hill town of Montalcino in southern Tuscany. Released no earlier than January of the fifth year after harvest, with at least two years in wood.

notes.name: Chianti Classico
notes.note: Historic heart of Chianti between Florence and Siena, symbolised by the black rooster. At least 80% Sangiovese. The top tier, Gran Selezione, can name one of the official sub-zones (UGA).

notes.name: Chianti
notes.note: Large Tuscan appellation surrounding Chianti Classico, mainly Sangiovese, with sub-zones such as Rufina and Colli Senesi.

notes.name: Vino Nobile di Montepulciano
notes.note: Sangiovese, locally called Prugnolo Gentile, from the town of Montepulciano in south-east Tuscany. Not related to the Montepulciano grape.

notes.name: Amarone della Valpolicella
notes.note: Dry red from grapes dried for months after harvest (appassimento), mainly Corvina, Corvinone and Rondinella, from the hills north of Verona.

notes.name: Recioto della Valpolicella
notes.note: The sweet, historic ancestor of Amarone, from the same dried grapes with fermentation stopped before all sugar turns to alcohol.

notes.name: Soave Superiore
notes.note: Garganega-based white from the hills east of Verona, often on volcanic basalt or limestone.

notes.name: Franciacorta
notes.note: Lombardy's traditional-method sparkling wine from Chardonnay, Pinot Nero and Pinot Bianco, with the local Erbamat also allowed, on moraine soils south of Lake Iseo.

notes.name: Conegliano Valdobbiadene - Prosecco
notes.note: The hilly heart of Prosecco Superiore in the Veneto, from Glera on steep 'hogback' slopes, a UNESCO World Heritage landscape since 2019. Cartizze is its most famous hill.

notes.name: Taurasi
notes.note: Aglianico from the hills of Irpinia near Avellino in Campania, often called the Barolo of the South for its tannin and longevity.

notes.name: Fiano di Avellino
notes.note: White Fiano from the Irpinia hills in Campania, with a long ageing potential unusual for southern whites.

notes.name: Greco di Tufo
notes.note: White Greco from eight communes around Tufo in Irpinia, where sulphur-rich soils were once mined.

notes.name: Montefalco Sagrantino
notes.note: Sagrantino from Montefalco in Umbria, one of the most tannic grapes in the world, made dry or as a sweet passito.

notes.name: Cerasuolo di Vittoria
notes.note: Sicily's only DOCG: a blend of Nero d'Avola and Frappato from the south-east of the island.

notes.name: Vermentino di Gallura
notes.note: Sardinia's only DOCG: Vermentino on granite soils in the north-east of the island.

notes.name: Gattinara
notes.note: Nebbiolo, locally called Spanna, from Alto Piemonte at the foot of the Alps, on acid volcanic soils.

notes.name: Ghemme
notes.note: Nebbiolo from Alto Piemonte on the east bank of the Sesia, facing Gattinara, on glacial moraine.

notes.name: Roero
notes.note: Sandy hills north of the Tanaro river opposite the Langhe, for Nebbiolo reds and Arneis whites.

notes.name: Gavi
notes.note: Cortese white from south-eastern Piedmont, near the Ligurian border. Also known as Cortese di Gavi.

notes.name: Asti
notes.note: Sweet, lightly sparkling Moscato Bianco from Piedmont, including the gentler Moscato d'Asti.

notes.name: Nizza
notes.note: Top tier of Barbera from 18 communes around Nizza Monferrato, a separate DOCG since 2014.

notes.name: Valtellina Superiore
notes.note: Nebbiolo, locally called Chiavennasca, on steep terraces along the Adda valley in the Alps of Lombardy.

notes.name: Sforzato di Valtellina
notes.note: Valtellina Nebbiolo made from dried grapes, similar in method to Amarone.

notes.name: Bolgheri
notes.note: Coastal Tuscan appellation where Bordeaux varieties made the area famous with Sassicaia and Ornellaia. Bolgheri Sassicaia has its own separate DOC.

notes.name: Etna
notes.note: Vineyards on the slopes of Europe's most active volcano in Sicily, up to about 1,000 m. Nerello Mascalese for reds, Carricante for whites. Producers name individual 'contrade'.

notes.name: Rioja
notes.note: Spain's first DOCa, since 1991, along the Ebro in La Rioja, Álava and Navarra. Mainly Tempranillo with Garnacha. Since 2017 labels can show zones, villages and 'viñedos singulares'.

notes.name: Priorat
notes.note: Catalan mountain region on llicorella, a dark slate, mostly Garnacha and Cariñena. One of only two Spanish appellations with Calificada status, alongside Rioja. Labels can name villages (vi de vila) and single sites (paratge).

notes.name: Ribera del Duero
notes.note: High plateau along the Duero in Castilla y León, mainly Tempranillo (Tinto Fino). Large swings between hot days and cold nights. Home of Vega Sicilia.

notes.name: Jerez-Xérès-Sherry
notes.note: Fortified wines from the triangle of Jerez, El Puerto de Santa María and Sanlúcar de Barrameda. Palomino on white albariza soil, aged in soleras, either under a veil of flor or oxidatively.

notes.name: Manzanilla-Sanlúcar de Barrameda
notes.note: The lightest style of sherry, aged under flor in the seaside town of Sanlúcar, where the sea air keeps the flor thick all year.

notes.name: Rías Baixas
notes.note: Atlantic Galicia, mainly Albariño, often trained on high pergolas to cope with humidity.

notes.name: Toro
notes.note: Hot, dry Castilla y León region for powerful Tinta de Toro, a local form of Tempranillo.

notes.name: Rueda
notes.note: Castilla y León's white-wine region, built on Verdejo.

notes.name: Bierzo
notes.note: North-western Castilla y León, for Mencía reds on slate and granite slopes.

notes.name: Jumilla
notes.note: South-eastern Spain, dry and high, built on Monastrell.

notes.name: Montilla-Moriles
notes.note: Andalusian wines similar to sherry, but Pedro Ximénez ripens so fully here that the wines often need no fortification.

notes.name: Cava
notes.note: Spanish traditional-method sparkling wine, made mostly in Penedès in Catalonia from Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada.

notes.name: Mosel
notes.note: Riesling on steep slate slopes along the Mosel, Saar and Ruwer. Some of the steepest vineyards in Europe. The light, low-alcohol style of Kabinett and Spätlese is world-famous.

notes.name: Rheingau
notes.note: A single south-facing slope along the Rhine where it flows west for about 30 km. Riesling dominates. Schloss Johannisberg and Kloster Eberbach shaped German wine history.

notes.name: Rheinhessen
notes.note: Germany's largest wine region, in rolling hills inside the bend of the Rhine. The Roter Hang at Nierstein and the limestone hills around Westhofen give its top wines.

notes.name: Pfalz
notes.note: Warm, sunny region along the Haardt mountains, the northern continuation of Alsace. Famous sites around Forst, Deidesheim and Wachenheim.

notes.name: Nahe
notes.note: Small region along the Nahe river with a great variety of soils, from volcanic rock to slate and sandstone.

notes.name: Ahr
notes.note: One of the northernmost red wine regions in the world, Spätburgunder on steep slate in a narrow valley. Badly hit by the floods of July 2021.

notes.name: Franken
notes.note: Bavarian region along the Main, known for Silvaner and the flat, round Bocksbeutel bottle.

notes.name: Baden
notes.note: Germany's warmest and most southerly region, from Lake Constance to Heidelberg. Strong in Pinot varieties, especially in the Kaiserstuhl.

notes.name: Württemberg
notes.note: Mainly red-wine region along the Neckar, with Trollinger and Lemberger.

notes.name: Mittelrhein
notes.note: Steep slate terraces in the Rhine gorge between Bingen and Bonn, part of the UNESCO Upper Middle Rhine Valley.

notes.name: Saale-Unstrut
notes.note: One of the northernmost quality wine regions of Europe, along the Saale and Unstrut rivers, on shell limestone.

notes.name: Sachsen
notes.note: Small eastern region along the Elbe around Dresden and Meissen.

notes.name: Hessische Bergstraße
notes.note: Germany's smallest region, on the warm western edge of the Odenwald.
Wehlener Sonnenuhr: steep slate slope across the Mosel from Wehlen, named after the sundial painted on a rock among the vines. One of the most famous Riesling sites in the world.

Bernkasteler Doctor: tiny, very steep site right above Bernkastel. Legend says its wine cured the Archbishop of Trier, Boemund II, in the 14th century. Among the most expensive vineyard land in Germany.
Graacher Himmelreich: large, steep slate slope between Bernkastel and Wehlen, known for elegant Riesling.
Erdener Treppchen: named after the steps carved into the slope to reach the terraces. Red and blue slate.
Ürziger Würzgarten: spectacularly steep site with an unusual red soil, very different from the grey slate around it. Known for spicy Riesling.
Piesporter Goldtröpfchen: south-facing amphitheatre of slate around Piesport, giving rich, fruity Riesling.
Brauneberger Juffer: long south-facing slope opposite Brauneberg, historically one of the most valued sites of the Mosel. Juffer-Sonnenuhr is its core.
Brauneberger Juffer-Sonnenuhr: the steepest, central part of the Juffer slope, with a sundial among the vines.
Forster Kirchenstück: small site behind the church of Forst, often ranked as the finest in the Pfalz. Basalt, limestone and sandstone in a warm, sheltered spot.
Forster Jesuitengarten: neighbour of Kirchenstück in Forst, once owned by the Jesuits.
Forster Pechstein: site named after the dark basalt in its soil, from an old volcanic outcrop above Forst.
Forster Ungeheuer: famous Forst site whose name means 'monster', with basalt and limestone soils.
Niederhäuser Hermannshöhle: steep site above the Nahe with a mix of slate, porphyry and volcanic rock. A reference Riesling site of the Nahe.
Schlossböckelheimer Kupfergrube: terraced site on a former copper mine, planted in the early 20th century by the Prussian state domain.
Schlossböckelheimer Felsenberg: volcanic rock site next to Kupfergrube on the Nahe.
Monzinger Halenberg: steep blue slate and quartzite site in the upper Nahe.
Niersteiner Pettenthal: steep part of the Roter Hang right above the Rhine, on red slate-like soil from the Permian (Rotliegend).
Niersteiner Hipping: part of the Roter Hang north of Nierstein, on red Rotliegend soil above the Rhine.
Niersteiner Ölberg: Roter Hang site above Nierstein, red soil, warm exposure.
Westhofener Morstein: limestone-rich site in the hills of southern Rheinhessen, famous for powerful dry Riesling.
Westhofener Kirchspiel: amphitheatre of limestone and marl in Westhofen, a neighbour of Morstein.
Dalsheimer Hubacker: limestone site in Flörsheim-Dalsheim, southern Rheinhessen.

notes.name: AOC Valais
notes.note: Switzerland's largest wine canton, in the dry upper Rhône valley protected by the Alps. Chasselas (called Fendant here) and Pinot Noir lead, with a wealth of native varieties: Petite Arvine, Amigne, Cornalin, Humagne Rouge and Heida.

notes.name: AOC Vaud
notes.note: Chasselas country on the shores of Lake Geneva. The terraces of Lavaux are a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2007, with Dézaley and Calamin as grand cru appellations. Also La Côte and Chablais.

notes.name: AOC Genève
notes.note: Switzerland's third wine canton, around the city and lake of Geneva. Gamay, Chasselas and a growing range of other varieties.

notes.name: AOC Neuchâtel
notes.note: Vineyards along Lake Neuchâtel at the foot of the Jura. Chasselas and Pinot Noir, and the pale rosé Oeil-de-Perdrix.

notes.name: DOC Ticino
notes.note: Italian-speaking Switzerland south of the Alps, where Merlot has been the main red grape since the early 20th century.

notes.name: AOC Graubünden
notes.note: Mountain canton whose Bündner Herrschaft, around Malans, Jenins, Maienfeld and Fläsch, makes some of Switzerland's best Pinot Noir, helped by the warm Föhn wind.

notes.name: AOC Zürich
notes.note: Vineyards around Lake Zürich and in the Weinland north of the city. Blauburgunder (Pinot Noir) and Räuschling, an old local white grape.

notes.name: AOC Schaffhausen
notes.note: Northern canton on the Rhine, known as Blauburgunderland for its Pinot Noir.

notes.name: Barossa Valley
notes.note: Warm valley north-east of Adelaide, settled by Silesian Lutherans in the 1840s. Some of the oldest Shiraz, Grenache and Mataro vines in the world survive here on their own roots, because phylloxera never reached South Australia.

notes.name: Eden Valley
notes.note: The higher, cooler hills east of the Barossa Valley, on granite and schist. Known for taut, lime-scented Riesling and for Shiraz from a few historic vineyards.

notes.name: McLaren Vale
notes.note: Maritime region south of Adelaide between the Mount Lofty Ranges and the Gulf St Vincent. Shiraz and Grenache dominate, and the region has mapped dozens of distinct geologies across its districts.

notes.name: Clare Valley
notes.note: A series of narrow valleys north of Adelaide, warm by day and cool at night. With Eden Valley it is Australia's classic home of dry Riesling.

notes.name: Coonawarra
notes.note: A strip about 12 to 15 km long of red terra rossa over limestone in the flat south-east of South Australia. It made its name with Cabernet Sauvignon.

notes.name: Adelaide Hills
notes.note: Cool, high part of the Mount Lofty Ranges just east of Adelaide. Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, and a base for sparkling wine.

notes.name: Margaret River
notes.note: Region in Western Australia between the Indian Ocean and the Leeuwin Ridge, planted from the late 1960s. The ocean keeps the climate mild; Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay are its best-known wines.

notes.name: Yarra Valley
notes.note: Cool region east of Melbourne, one of the first vineyard areas of Victoria in the 1830s. Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and sparkling wine, with Shiraz on warmer sites.

notes.name: Mornington Peninsula
notes.note: Maritime peninsula south of Melbourne with small vineyards, surrounded by sea on three sides. Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

notes.name: Heathcote
notes.note: Central Victorian region on red Cambrian soils along the Mount Camel Range, best known for dense Shiraz.

notes.name: Rutherglen
notes.note: North-east Victoria, hot and dry, famous for fortified Muscat and Topaque aged for decades in a solera-like system.

notes.name: Great Southern
notes.note: Australia's largest wine region, on the south coast of Western Australia. Five subregions: Albany, Denmark, Frankland River, Mount Barker and Porongurup. Riesling, Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon.

notes.name: Tasmania
notes.note: The island state is a single wine GI. Australia's coolest wine region, increasingly important for sparkling wine, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

notes.name: Canberra District
notes.note: Cool upland region around the national capital, mostly in New South Wales. Known for Shiraz, often co-fermented with a little Viognier, and for Riesling.

notes.name: Hunter
notes.note: One of Australia's oldest wine regions, north of Sydney. Humid and warm, it makes a unique style of low-alcohol Semillon that ages for decades, and medium-bodied Shiraz.

notes.name: Orange
notes.note: High-altitude region on the slopes of the extinct volcano Mount Canobolas in New South Wales. Its lower boundary is set at 600 m.

notes.name: Riverland
notes.note: Irrigated region along the Murray River, one of the largest sources of Australian wine by volume.

notes.name: Marlborough
notes.note: At the north-east tip of the South Island, New Zealand's largest wine region. Its pungent Sauvignon Blanc, first planted in the 1970s, put the country on the wine map. The Wairau and Awatere valleys are its main parts.

notes.name: Central Otago
notes.note: The world's most southerly major wine region, inland on the South Island with a continental climate. Pinot Noir on schist-derived soils is its signature.

notes.name: Hawke's Bay
notes.note: East coast of the North Island, warm and sunny, the country's second-largest region. Syrah and Bordeaux varieties, notably from the Gimblett Gravels, an old riverbed.

notes.name: Wairarapa
notes.note: Region in the south-east of the North Island, including Martinborough. Small producers, best known for Pinot Noir.

notes.name: Martinborough
notes.note: Small town and terrace of free-draining gravels in the Wairarapa, among New Zealand's first Pinot Noir areas in the 1980s.

notes.name: Waiheke Island
notes.note: Island in the Hauraki Gulf off Auckland with a warm, maritime climate, known for Bordeaux-style reds and Syrah.

notes.name: Gisborne
notes.note: On the east coast of the North Island, warm and fertile, long known for Chardonnay.

notes.name: Nelson
notes.note: Sunny region at the top of the South Island, west of Marlborough. Aromatic whites and Pinot Noir from the Waimea Plains and the Moutere Hills.

notes.name: North Canterbury
notes.note: The main wine area of Canterbury, centred on the Waipara Valley north of Christchurch. Riesling, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay on limestone and gravel.

notes.name: Stellenbosch
notes.note: The heart of South African wine, east of Cape Town between the Simonsberg, Helderberg and Jonkershoek mountains. Cabernet Sauvignon, Bordeaux blends, Pinotage and Chenin Blanc on granite and sandstone soils. The district is divided into wards.

notes.name: Swartland
notes.note: Rolling wheat and vine country north of Cape Town, dry-farmed bush vines on shale and granite. Since the 2000s a centre of old-vine Chenin Blanc and Rhône-style blends.

notes.name: Constantia
notes.note: The oldest wine area of the Cape, on the slopes of the Constantiaberg south of Cape Town. Its sweet Vin de Constance was famous in 18th- and 19th-century Europe.

notes.name: Franschhoek
notes.note: Valley settled by French Huguenots in the late 17th century, enclosed by mountains east of Paarl.

notes.name: Walker Bay
notes.note: Cool maritime district around Hermanus, including the Hemel-en-Aarde wards, known for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

notes.name: Elgin
notes.note: Cool, high apple-growing basin in the Overberg, a source of Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

notes.name: Paarl
notes.note: Large district around the town of Paarl and its granite domes, north of Stellenbosch, home of the KWV for most of the 20th century.

notes.name: Robertson
notes.note: Warm, dry Breede River valley district on lime-rich soils, known for Chardonnay and sparkling Cap Classique.

notes.name: Coastal Region
notes.note: Wine of Origin region that groups the districts close to the Atlantic and False Bay, including Stellenbosch, Paarl, Swartland and Cape Town.

notes.name: Valle del Maipo
notes.note: The valley around Santiago, cradle of Chilean wine in the 19th century. Alto Maipo, at the foot of the Andes, is known for Cabernet Sauvignon.

notes.name: Valle de Colchagua
notes.note: Part of the Rapel Valley, warm and sunny, best known for Carmenère, Cabernet Sauvignon and blends. Apalta, a horseshoe of hillside vineyards, is its most famous sector.

notes.name: Valle de Casablanca
notes.note: Coastal valley between Santiago and Valparaíso, cooled by the Pacific and the Humboldt current. Planted from the 1980s with Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

notes.name: Valle de Leyda
notes.note: Coastal zone of the San Antonio Valley, a few kilometres from the ocean, for cool-climate Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir.

notes.name: Valle del Maule
notes.note: Chile's largest wine-growing valley by area, with old dry-farmed Carignan and País vines in its coastal hills.

notes.name: Valle del Itata
notes.note: One of the oldest vineyard areas of Chile, in the south, with dry-farmed old País, Muscat and Cinsault vines on granite slopes.

notes.name: Valle del Elqui
notes.note: Northern valley in the Andes foothills, very dry and clear, best known for pisco but also for high-altitude Syrah and Sauvignon Blanc.

notes.name: Valle del Aconcagua
notes.note: Valley north of Santiago, warm inland, with coastal vineyards reaching towards the Pacific.

notes.name: Apalta
notes.note: Horseshoe of steep hillsides in the Colchagua Valley on the north bank of the Tinguiririca river, home to some of Chile's best-known reds.

notes.name: Mendoza
notes.note: Argentina's main wine province, producing most of the country's wine in an irrigated high desert at the foot of the Andes. Malbec is its signature.

notes.name: Luján de Cuyo
notes.note: Department south of Mendoza city with some of the oldest Malbec vineyards, between about 900 and 1,100 m. It holds one of Argentina's two DOCs.

notes.name: Valle de Uco
notes.note: High valley south-west of Mendoza (Tupungato, Tunuyán and San Carlos), with vineyards from about 900 m to over 1,500 m. Cool nights and alluvial soils.

notes.name: Paraje Altamira
notes.note: Alluvial fan of the Tunuyán river in San Carlos, Valle de Uco, at around 1,000 to 1,100 m. Stony, calcareous soils; registered as an IG in 2013 and enlarged in 2017.

notes.name: Los Chacayes
notes.note: High IG in Tunuyán, Valle de Uco, on stony alluvial soils up towards the Andes.

notes.name: Agrelo
notes.note: District of Luján de Cuyo with deep clay-loam soils, widely planted with Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon.

notes.name: San Juan
notes.note: Hot, dry province north of Mendoza, Argentina's second wine region by volume. Syrah does well here, especially in the Tulum and Pedernal valleys.

notes.name: Salta
notes.note: Northern province whose Calchaquí valleys hold some of the highest vineyards in the world, above 2,000 m in places. Torrontés and intense Malbec.

notes.name: Cafayate - Valle de Cafayate
notes.note: The best-known part of the Calchaquí valleys, around 1,700 m, sandy and dry. Home of aromatic Torrontés.

notes.name: Patagonia - Patagonia Argentina
notes.note: The southern wine regions along the Río Negro and Neuquén valleys and further south, cool and windy, for Pinot Noir and Malbec.

notes.name: Vale dos Vinhedos
notes.note: Valley in the Serra Gaúcha of Rio Grande do Sul, settled by Italian immigrants in the 1870s. Brazil's first wine IP (2002) and first DO (2012).

notes.name: Campanha Gaúcha
notes.note: Plains along the Uruguayan border in Rio Grande do Sul, drier and sunnier than the Serra Gaúcha.

notes.name: Vale do São Francisco
notes.note: Tropical irrigated vineyards around Petrolina at about 9° south, which can harvest more than once a year.

notes.name: Metropolitana
notes.note: The departments around Montevideo, chiefly Canelones, where most Uruguayan wine is made. Tannat is the national grape.

notes.name: Niagara Peninsula
notes.note: Ontario's main wine area, between Lake Ontario and Lake Erie, moderated by the lakes and sheltered by the Niagara Escarpment. Icewine, Riesling, Chardonnay and Cabernet Franc.

notes.name: Okanagan Valley
notes.note: Long valley of glacial lakes in British Columbia, semi-desert in the south around Osoyoos and Oliver, cooler in the north.

notes.name: Prince Edward County
notes.note: Limestone peninsula in Lake Ontario where vines are buried in winter to survive the cold. Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

notes.name: Kakheti
notes.note: Eastern Georgia along the Alazani valley, where most of the country's wine is made, including amber wines fermented with skins in buried clay qvevri, a method inscribed by UNESCO in 2013.

notes.name: Tsinandali
notes.note: Village appellation in Kakheti for a dry white blend of Rkatsiteli and Mtsvane, named after the village of Tsinandali, home of the estate of the poet Alexander Chavchavadze.

notes.name: Mukuzani
notes.note: Appellation in Kakheti for dry red Saperavi from the right bank of the Alazani.

notes.name: Kindzmarauli
notes.note: Appellation in Kvareli, Kakheti, for semi-sweet red Saperavi.

notes.name: Khvanchkara
notes.note: Appellation in Racha, western Georgia, for naturally semi-sweet red wine from Aleksandrouli and Mujuretuli.

notes.name: Codru
notes.note: The central, wooded hill region of Moldova around Chișinău, with the country's large underground cellars at Cricova and Mileștii Mici.

notes.name: Bekaa Valley
notes.note: High plateau between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon mountains at about 1,000 m, where nearly all Lebanese wine is made.

notes.name: Galilee
notes.note: Israel's northern wine region, highest and coolest, including Upper Galilee.

notes.name: Thrace-Marmara
notes.note: European Turkey and the Sea of Marmara coast, one of the country's main wine areas, second in output to the Aegean.

notes.name: Central Anatolia (Cappadocia)
notes.note: Volcanic high plateau around Nevşehir where vines have been grown for thousands of years. Native grapes such as Emir in Cappadocia and Kalecik Karası from Kalecik near Ankara.

notes.name: Yamanashi
notes.note: Prefecture west of Tokyo and the centre of Japanese wine since the 19th century. Its signature is Koshu, a pink-skinned grape for delicate dry whites.

notes.name: Hokkaido
notes.note: Japan's northern island, cool enough for Pinot Noir and German varieties, with fast-growing plantings.

notes.name: Helan Mountain East (Ningxia)
notes.note: Desert foothills of the Helan Mountains in Ningxia, sheltered from Gobi winds. Vines are buried each winter against the cold. China's best-known region for Cabernet Sauvignon.

notes.name: Yantai
notes.note: Coastal area of Shandong where Changyu founded China's first modern winery in 1892.

notes.name: Nashik Valley
notes.note: Plateau north-east of Mumbai at 500 to 700 m that produces most of India's wine. Vines are pruned so that the harvest falls in the dry winter months.
